rules.coverage_note: The manifest states the dependency. The resolved version and the enabled feature set are Cargo's, not the overlay's.

One Router entity per function that calls a Router builder method, keyed by that function. `receiver` is the expression the builder was chained onto, as written. A router assembled across two functions is two entities: omega-rust states no value flow and the overlay may not invent it.

The URL a route serves. `.route("/users/{id}", get(show))` states it as the first argument, and `{normalized_route}` makes `/users/{id}`, `/users/:id` and `/users/[id]` one identity shared with every other HTTP framework here. The method is not part of the key: the verb is a second fact, and a chained builder's call_expression spans every earlier link of the chain, so a span join from the verb to its own `.route(` would bind every later `.route(` too. The method-router expression is published verbatim as `methods` instead.

The handler a registration names -- `get(handlers::show_user)` -- keyed by the name it is declared under, so the route in main.rs meets the `async fn` in another module. `handles` runs from the route the enclosing `.route(...)` states to that handler.

The handler a registration names -- `get(handlers::show_user)` -- keyed by the name it is declared under, so the route in main.rs meets the `async fn` in another module. `handles` runs from the route the enclosing `.route(...)` states to that handler.

The handler a registration names -- `get(handlers::show_user)` -- keyed by the name it is declared under, so the route in main.rs meets the `async fn` in another module. `handles` runs from the route the enclosing `.route(...)` states to that handler.

An axum handler is recognised by the extractor and response types in its signature, which the `definition.function` span covers. A handler taking no extractor and returning `&'static str` is not recognised here; it is still minted by the route-registration rules when a route names it.

`.nest("/api", api_router())` states both ends now: `prefix` is the URL prefix the sub-router is mounted under and `mounted` is the expression that produced it, as written. `merge` takes no prefix, so its `prefix` is the merged expression and `mount_kind` is what tells the two apart.

`layer` wraps every route on the router including the fallback; `route_layer` runs only when a route matched. The applied value is named now -- `TraceLayer::new_for_http()`, `middleware::from_fn(auth)` -- as the expression text, which is what was written rather than a resolved type.

An import states which tower / tower-http layer or axum middleware constructor this crate uses. Which call site applies it is `axum.router.middleware`'s `layer` attribute, as written text; the two are not joined, because the applied value is an expression and not a resolved type.

`with_state` is where shared state is attached and the router's state type becomes (). `state` is the value handed to it, as written; the type it is extracted as in a handler signature is the `State<..>` of axum.handler.declaration.
What catches an unmatched request, and what answers it: `fallback` is the handler, tower service or 405 responder named at the call site, as written.

The hand-off from Router to hyper. `router` is the expression the Router came from, as written -- `app()` -- and `_with_connect_info` is the spelling that makes `ConnectInfo` available to handlers, which is why the two names are kept apart.

`axum::serve(listener, app)` is the 0.7 entrypoint and arrives as `call.path` named `serve`. Both arguments are stated: `listener` is the bound TcpListener expression and `served` is the service handed to it, which is where `main` names the router-building function.

gaps: the HTTP method of a route is not part of its identity: the URL is the first argument of .route(..) and the verb is a separate call fact, and a chained builder's call_expression contains every earlier link of the chain, so a span join from the verb to its own .route( would bind every later .route( as well; the URL entity is keyed http:*: and the method-router expression is published as the Route attribute methods

a handler is named as written -- show_user, handlers::show_user, an inline closure -- and is not resolved to a declaration, so a route registered with a qualified path and the same handler declared in another module are two Handler keys
an applied layer is the expression text of the argument (TraceLayer::new_for_http()), not the type it constructs, so it cannot be joined to the use that imported that type

on(MethodFilter::GET, handler) and on_service take the method filter as their first argument and the handler as their second, so they are excluded from the handler rules rather than made to name MethodFilter::GET as a handler
a route whose URL is not a string literal -- .route(&format!("{prefix}/x"), ..) -- keys on the expression text: the Pack captures the argument as written and does not evaluate it
middleware/state/merge/fallback/service registrations are authored configuration, not proof of runtime invocation
